title: 79 Promoting extension scholarship and navigating the tenure and promotion process in extension
content:
Abstract
Promoting Extension scholarship and successfully navigating the tenure and promotion process in Extension require a strategic approach that integrates educational resources, program development, implementation and impact assessment. Extension scholarship can encompass activities such as curriculum development, peer-reviewed publications, and innovative teaching and research methodologies, and program evaluation. The tenure and promotion process for Extension faculty places significant emphasis on demonstrating impact through both measurable outcomes for constituents served and scholarly outputs. Extension faculty engage in on-farm research trials, collaborate with producers to test innovative practices, and disseminate results through Extension workshops, field days, and digital media. These activities contribute to the broader Extension knowledge base while also providing materials suitable for tenure and promotion. For faculty navigating tenure and promotion in Extension, it is crucial to develop a well-documented record of scholarly contributions. This includes Extension publications, grantsmanship, conference presentations, curriculum developed, program leadership and impact assessments. Furthermore, interdisciplinary collaboration strengthens Extension scholarship by fostering innovative approaches to problem-solving. Active collaborations within or outside of the institution creates a broader network of resources to help address producer questions, especially when many issues are shared and complex in nature. Additional measures of Extension program success may also include client interactions, communication consistency and responsiveness, one-on-one or group trainings with Extension agents and farmers, and managerial oversight of programs. It is important that these outputs are evaluated and critiqued in the tenure and promotion process with context to the faculty member’s Extension appointment and target audiences of interest. The same metrics used to assess research may not fit scholarly expectations of the Extension appointment. A general misperception is that Extension cannot be evaluated or easily understood in the promotion and tenure process relative to research, teaching, or service. This is where ‘impacts’ and ‘outputs’ are sometimes misconstrued to mean the same thing, where outputs tend to be more tangible, whereas impacts are harder to quantify. True impacts require 1) measurable goals and goal setting for the Extension program, and 2) a multi-faceted approach for collecting feedback on Extension programs. Feedback through needs assessments, pre- and post-program surveys, case studies, testimonials, and stakeholder data are ways to generate this. Extension program effectiveness and annual employee evaluation should incorporate input from Extension constituents, direct reports for Extension employees, district/team leadership and administration, and stakeholders. Extension programs are a key part of scholarship portfolios for faculty at land-grant institutions, which positions our programs to continue making real-world impacts and generating solutions for agricultural operations.
